introduction: “Justice consists in rendering to each his due … bounty consists in rewarding him even when he has done no work.” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s distinction, illustrated by a workman and his wage, runs through all these readings. With God we ask for bounty, since no one could stand before strict justice. Among people the readings draw a second line, which is the centre of the guide: an individual who is wronged must forgive and may not avenge himself, but society has no right to forgive on the victims’ behalf; it must punish to protect, and “reward and punishment” are the two pillars of order. A universal amnesty would undo the world. Punishment rightly given is a form of education, and a just government is the best friend of the oppressed. The pairing is as old as scripture: Micah’s “do justly … love mercy,” the Sinai Name that forgives and does not clear the guilty, and Paul, who writes “avenge not yourselves” and, a few lines later, that the ruler “beareth not the sword in vain.” The parable of the labourers is ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s own example in other dress. The elder brother and Jonah speak for justice offended by mercy; Socrates for no retaliation at all; and Paul’s “by one man sin entered” is the text behind the doctrine one reading rejects.
questions: State the difference between justice and bounty in your own words, with an example from ordinary life other than wages.
“If someone transgresses against you personally, you should forgive them. But if they transgress against everyone, you cannot forgive everyone’s right.” Where does this line fall in a case you know?
Punishment by a just authority is called “a form of mercy.” What makes punishment educative and not merely painful?
The elder brother and Jonah are both angry at mercy. What is right in their complaint, and what do the stories answer?
We are told to pray that God “not decree justice” for us. What does that prayer imply about how we should judge others?
“Kindness cannot be shown the tyrant.” How would you tell a person who can be won by kindness from one who is only encouraged by it?

outside.why: Justice “is not equality, but the giving to everyone according to his right.” The oldest definition in philosophy, as Socrates reports it: justice is the giving to each man what is proper to him.
The reading joins justice to mercy as two attributes of one God. Micah joins them as two duties of one person: to do justly, and to love mercy.

Justice pays the workman his wage; “bounty consists in rewarding him even when he has done no work.” The householder in the parable paid the last hired a full day: friend, I do thee no wrong: didst not thou agree with me for a penny?
The elder brother states the case for justice against such bounty: lo, these many years do I serve thee, and yet thou never gavest me a kid. What would you say to him?
Favours given by merit are justice; guidance is “a supreme” bounty. Paul: by grace are ye saved through faith; not of works, lest any man should boast.
Ask that God “open the gate of bounty and not decree justice.” The psalmist’s prayer: enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified.
Another psalm: if thou, Lord, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand? But there is forgiveness with thee.
“Mercy gives bounty without regard to merits.” Portia: in the course of justice, none of us should see salvation: we do pray for mercy.
Mercy falls “upon whomsoever God wishes.” Paul quotes Exodus: I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy.
Obeying the commandments “has nothing to do with Mercy, but is Obedience.” Jesus: when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants.
“If someone transgresses against you personally, you should forgive them.” Paul: avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath.
But “the social body must rise up to defend and protect.” Paul makes the same division in the next chapter: the ruler is the minister of God to thee for good; he beareth not the sword in vain.
The individual “must forgive, just as God forgives.” Peter asked how often, and was told: I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.
The saying the reading has in view: ye have heard, An eye for an eye. But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil.
Individuals have no right to vengeance, yet “reward and punishment must be carried out.” The Qur’án on why a community punishes: there is life for you in retaliation, O men of understanding.
The heir may not take the matter into his own hands; the government may punish, and pardon is better. The Qur’án: the life for the life. But whoso forgoeth it, it shall be expiation for him.
And: whosoever pardoneth and amendeth, his wage is the affair of Allah.
A just government saves “the predators from their predatory nature” and consoles the oppressed. The psalm: give the king thy judgments, O God. He shall judge thy poor with judgment.

“Kindness cannot be shown the tyrant, the deceiver, or the thief”; it confirms them. Ecclesiastes: because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.
Paul gives the opposite counsel to individuals: if thine enemy hunger, feed him; overcome evil with good. Which wrongdoers, on the readings’ account, are reached by kindness, and which are not?
Chastisement carried out by law, without selfish motive, is “the cause of good.” Hebrews: whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth.
Soldiers forced into a war they did not choose are treated “with His mercy, not with His justice.” The psalm: he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust.

A general amnesty “in all countries” would throw the world into disarray. Socrates, in prison, held to a rule without exceptions: we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered from him. How do the readings keep his rule for persons and deny it to the state? Is the distinction secure?
The law must punish “to prevent a repetition.” The old law of proportion, which limited vengeance to the measure of the wrong: eye for eye, tooth for tooth.
Could Justice itself punish Adam’s posterity for Adam’s sin? Ezekiel: all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die.

The doctrine in question rests on Paul: by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men. How does ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s appeal to justice bear on this verse, and what else might Paul mean?
People must be held “through fear and hope”: none should despair of forgiveness, and all should fear to sin. The psalm: he hath not dealt with us after our sins.
The Name proclaimed on Sinai holds both: forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty.
A father’s punishment “is actually a form of mercy.” Proverbs: he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes.
“Although it appears as wrath yet in” reality it is kindness. Lamentations: he doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men.
“That which traineth the world is Justice … upheld by two pillars, reward and punishment.” Proverbs: the king by judgment establisheth the land.
Kings have no helper “mightier than justice and wisdom.” David’s last words: he that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God.
Augustine: justice being taken away, then, what are kingdoms but great robberies?
Judges who weighed the spiritual consequences of their rulings would be “Divine agents.” Moses to the judges: ye shall not be afraid of the face of man; for the judgment is God’s.
A governor may rule justly or as a tyrant; he has been given laws. Pascal: justice without might is helpless; might without justice is tyrannical.
A tribunal that “will decide between kings and kings.” Isaiah: he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares.
“The law is the same for the poor as for the rich.” Leviticus: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty.
Happiness lies in “giving every class of creation its due right.” Aristotle: justice is often thought to be the greatest of virtues.
A government should be “a true shepherd.” Ezekiel has God say what that is: I will seek that which was lost, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick.

Is it ever right to rebel? “Yes, if he deals unjustly and tyrannically … he forfeits the right to govern.” Locke: whenever the legislators endeavour to reduce them to slavery under arbitrary power, they put themselves into a state of war with the people.

Paul seems to leave no such opening: let every soul be subject unto the higher powers; the powers that be are ordained of God. Other readings in this collection ask believers to obey their governments. How do you read this answer beside them?
Nations did not act with justice, and a war swept away the old order. Lincoln on another such reckoning: the judgments of the Lord are true and righteous altogether.
A general proposes to treat an invading army as guests. Proverbs: if thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat.
“Then the Balances of Divine Justice will be set up.” The writing on Belshazzar’s wall: thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting.
“Justice and fairness have vanished from the world.” Isaiah: judgment is turned away backward, and justice standeth afar off.
The oppressors have surrounded the people of truth. Habakkuk: O Lord, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! even cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save!
“Pray for him … that He may ever confirm him in justice.” Paul: I exhort that prayers be made for kings, and for all that are in authority.
“Command the people to justice and piety.” Isaiah: learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed.

“They are like unto mere children, and our Lord is the Educator.” He could seize them with a word, and withholds. The psalmist on a lifetime of watching: I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken.

God spared Nineveh, and His prophet was furious: it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry. Have you ever resented mercy shown to someone who, in justice, deserved otherwise? What does the book of Jonah say to that?
“He dealeth with grace after justice hath appeared.” James: mercy rejoiceth against judgment.
“Consider ye the justice of God and His mercy which encompasseth the worlds.” The psalm sees them meet: mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other.
“When Thou showest justice there is trepidation.” Isabella, pleading for her brother: how would you be, if He, which is the top of judgment, should but judge you as you are?
A prayer “by the sovereignty of Thy forgiveness which encompasses all created things.” The Qur’án: My mercy embraceth all things.
Portia: the quality of mercy is not strain’d, it droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven upon the place beneath.

plato-giving-to-each-man-what-is-proper-.text: he really meant to say that justice is the giving to each man what is proper to him, and this he termed a debt
